body.text: You're standing in the first aisle of your local supermarket.
The lights are bright, the music aggressively cheerful. You are armed with your shopping list of essentials for the week, plus an empty trolley and a good dose of optimism.
Today, you are going to buy healthy, nutritious food within your budget. You have half an hour.
You begin. But before long, your head is buzzing with questions.
What counts as a healthy snack? What kind of cereal is tasty but not full of sugar? Which yoghurt will satisfy the picky eater in the house? Do you really need extra protein in everything?
You select your usual brand of snack bars, packed with protein and promises of "no nasties".
But is this product actually good for you? Let's take a look.
Note: This article contains general information only. For personal advice, consult a qualified professional.
There's a lot going on here. What if we stripped it back?
Let's add labels step by step, starting with factual, regulated information (no marketing claims allowed).
This information legally has to be included on most packaging, according to the Food Standards Code set by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) and Australian consumer law.
The product's name. This must be an accurate description.
The supplier's name and address, the country of origin, and the batch number. These ensure a product is traceable.
A use-by or best-before date, storage conditions and directions for use.
Allergens must also be shown.
This is a useful one: the ingredients list.
Most packaged foods have to list all ingredients in descending order of weight. That means the order of the ingredients can be as important as the ingredients themselves.
The list must also show the percentage of the key ingredients in a food.
This snack bar is banana-flavoured, so the percentage of banana is shown in the list.
Now we come to the nutrition panel.
This is where you can see key health measures like energy, protein, fat, and carbs, both in a single serve and in 100 grams or millilitres of the food or drink.
Most packaged products must display a nutrition panel.
So what should you pay attention to?
At first glance, it can be hard to make sense of an ingredient list, but dieticians recommend focusing on three simple questions:
• What's the main ingredient?
• How recognisable are the ingredients?
Alexandra Jones, a public health lawyer at the George Institute for Global Health, says the characterising ingredient in a product should be easy to identify and have a reasonably high percentage.
"If it says strawberry yoghurt on the front, then where it has strawberry on the back [in the ingredients list], it has to say what percentage," she explains.
"This is to stop, for example, something saying it's vegetable juice, but then you see it's only got 2 per cent vegetables and it's 98 per cent orange."

Food producers may also lower the proportion of an ingredient to cut costs, which is why some tinned tomatoes contain 98 per cent tomato, compared to 60 per cent in others (usually supplemented with additives and concentrated purees).
If the list is long and the ingredients hard to understand, the product is likely an ultra-processed food (UPF).
There's some debate among scientists about what exactly constitutes a UPF, but a commonly used definition comes from an internationally recognised classification system called NOVA:
Ultra-processed foods … are not modified foods but formulations made mostly or entirely from substances derived from foods and additives, with little if any intact [whole] food.
UPFs are not all bad for you — some foods require additives to stay fresh, for example — but health experts say there are several reasons we should treat them with caution.
• As a category, UPFs tend to be high in sugar, fat and salt
• They're often hyper-palatable and high-calorie
• They tend to replace other, healthier foods we should be eating more of
• Early research points to some of the additives common in UPFs being linked to poor health outcomes
A 2026 study analysing the health of almost 9 million people linked high consumption of UPFs to several serious health risks, including heart disease, diabetes, cancer and anxiety.

"Everyone should be looking to cut back on their intake of ultra-processed foods, and the only way that you can really do that as an everyday consumer is to flip over a product and have a look at the ingredients list," says Daisy Coyle, a dietitian and public health expert at the George Institute for Global Health.
"It's not a fail-proof method, but it's a pretty good way to tell, particularly when the ingredients list looks like a paragraph."
For many Australians, UPFs are a practical option due to their lower cost, longer shelf life and convenience, explains dietician and Adelaide University associate professor Evangeline Mantzioris.
In these cases, she suggests people take manageable steps to balance ultra-processed and whole foods where possible.
For example, if ultra-processed bread helps entice a child to eat a salad sandwich, it's a net win, she says.
Dr Mantzioris says many of the supermarket's more cost-effective options can be nutritious.
"Frozen and canned fruit and vegetables are actually quite a good option because they have been preserved by either freezing or canning, so generally don't have things added to them," she says.
"Canned legumes and chickpeas are incredibly cheap and healthy. You can buy them for 95 cents a can."
How about the nutrition panel?
Dr Coyle says the nutrition information panel is a powerful tool for consumers.
"It tells you basically all you need to know about a product," she says.
"The thing is, people don't understand how to use it."
She says in most cases, we should pay more attention to the 100-gram or millilitre column, rather than the serving size column.

"The per serving is confusing because manufacturers or food companies can choose what the serving size is, so if you're using that to guide your decision making, you're not comparing apples to apples," she says.
Dr Coyle says the key metrics we should be paying attention to are salt, fat and sugar.
To see the recommended amounts to check for, head to our supermarket survival guide — it's a cheat sheet to keep handy in the supermarket.
It's not just words that entice us to buy. Pictures and colours can have a subconscious effect, too.
Let's look at some of the enticing designs on our snack bar box.
Fresh banana, oats and a hand-written look — how earthy! But does what's on the box match what's in it?
Other elements, like stories about the brand or sustainability messages, can also suggest a product is healthy, regardless of what it contains.
Let's take a look at the Health Star Rating. This is a government-led labelling system that rates the overall nutrition of a product from 0.5 stars to five.

A product's Health Star Rating is decided based on an algorithm that weighs up key nutrition measures within a given category. It was designed by the Australian and New Zealand governments, in collaboration with the food industry, public health experts and consumer groups.
Can you trust the Health Star Rating?

Products can lose points for high levels of saturated fat, sodium and sugar, and gain points for fibre, protein, fruits, vegetables, nuts and legumes. A Health Star Rating calculator is publicly available.
Critically though, the Health Star Rating is entirely voluntary.
As of the end of 2025, only 39 per cent of products in Australia displayed a Health Star Rating.

In February 2026, Food Ministers — a group of state and territory ministers from health and related portfolios — voted to make the Health Star Rating mandatory for all products. This proposal is currently in the consultation phase.

Critics say food producers can game the system by adding certain nutrients, like protein, that boost the star rating but don't actually make the food healthier. Some are also sceptical of the system given the involvement of food companies in shaping its algorithm.
Other health experts say the Health Star Rating may not be perfect, but it can still be a useful tool to help consumers compare products, and could be improved once it was made mandatory.
"We've done many, many papers on this and we think it does work well overall; we think consumers can generally understand it," Dr Jones says.
"If it genuinely incentivises companies to improve the product by cutting out salt and sugar to get a better star rating, then this benefits everyone, including people who don't read labels.
"We just need to make sure that the way it's designed means they can't just sub in something else."
See if you can correctly guess the Health Star Rating that food companies have put on their products below.
Back to the box. Let's take a look at some of the claims on the front. What can we trust here?
There are many different claims here …
… from nutrition benefits like "source of fibre" to the much more vague "no nasties".
The back holds more promises of "real banana" — which is technically true, as we spotted 3 per cent banana puree concentrate in the ingredient list.
Welcome to the wild west of packaging claims.
The real meaning of 'no nasties'
In Australia, claims like no nasties, natural, pure, clean, superfood and guilt-free are purely marketing terms.
None of these claims mean the product is necessarily healthy, nutritious or not ultra-processed.
"[These terms] are used everywhere … A lot of them are so vague they don't mean anything," Dr Jones says.
"Like, what does natural mean? … It's got no legal meaning.
"Asbestos is natural, mercury is natural, sugar is natural — that doesn't mean it's good for you."
Other claims, like cholesterol-free, multi-grain, or "baked, not fried", are based in fact, but can be used misleadingly to imply a product is healthier than it is.

The term "organic" also doesn't indicate anything about how a food was made or what it contains — a food can be labelled organic and still be ultra-processed (although if a product claims to be "certified organic", it must be able to prove certification according to Australian consumer law).
The only way to see through these claims, health experts say, is to look at the ingredients and nutrition panel.
And the most common place in the supermarket to find these claims? The health food aisle.
"The lolly aisle and chips — everyone knows they're bad. But the health food aisle is the most misleading," Dr Mantzioris says.
"It's the muesli bars, the cereal, some of those ready-to-eat meals.
"The more claims that are on there, the more you should be careful."
What about other claims?
"Source of fibre"
Certain claims about nutrition or health benefits, like fibre, are controlled by the Australian food regulator, FSANZ.

That includes claims about certain nutrients, based on a list of rules. For example, our protein bar can say "source of fibre", as it contains at least 2 grams of fibre per serving, but is not allowed to say "good source of fibre", which requires 7 grams per serving.

The regulator also requires food companies to notify the CEO of FSANZ before making a specific health claim on food packaging or in advertising (for example, claiming a product supports emotional wellbeing or maintains healthy bowel function).
However, it maintains no responsibility for verifying, approving or enforcing those claims.
"11g of protein"
It seems "protein" is emblazoned on almost every packaged food at the moment. Our snack bar has 11 grams!
(That's a little less than two eggs and a little more than 100 grams of Greek yoghurt).
Dr Jones says it's more of a fad than a dietary need.
"This obsession with protein right now doesn't necessarily match the evidence," she says.
"That's just a marketing claim that's everywhere."
Dr Coyle agrees that most people, especially if they're not elderly, don't need additional protein.
"Most people meet their protein requirements," she says.
"Obviously there are certain people in the population that have higher protein requirements, but that's not something that we would be looking to encourage at a population [level]."
"Natural sugars"
Claims about sugar can also be misleading. In Australia, food companies don't have to differentiate between natural and added sugars in the nutrition panel of their packaging.
Dr Coyle says this can mean that sugar "slips through the cracks".
"It's not always immediately obvious that a product is high in sugar, because sugar doesn't just come from sugar itself, it can come from things like honey or fruit juice concentrates," she says.
"There are some marketing claims that are used to make a product look like it's got healthy sources of sugar, when really they have the same effect on your body.
"The best thing you can do is just try and limit your total sugar intake altogether."
So, who's in charge?
Well, FSANZ establishes the Food Standards Code, and if a food company breaches it, it's up to state and territory food authorities to take action.
In cases of misleading advertising, that falls to the ACCC, Australia's consumer watchdog, as well as state and territory consumer protection agencies.
But often, problematic marketing goes unchallenged, Dr Jones says.
"[Regulators] are more focused on stopping overnight food poisoning, not what I call long-term food poisoning, which is what you get if you eat a diet high in things you don't need," she says.
Research shows that Australians often assume food packaging is more tightly regulated than it actually is, Dr Coyle says.
"Consumers are pretty trusting," she says.
"Their understanding of [what is and isn't regulated] is not very strong, and it shouldn't have to be.
"Consumers should be motivated to make healthy choices, but it shouldn't be hard for them to do that. And right now it really is."
Dr Jones says it can be empowering for people to see through marketing spin.
"I think it's useful to give people hope that they can vote with their fork or their trolley … especially if it helps them not get ripped off," she says.

"But at the same time, I often think of the analogy of a goldfish in polluted water. We're in such a challenging environment that even a really motivated person is going to be constantly receiving signals that point you in the [wrong] direction.
"We really need to change other elements of the system, and ideally have a healthier food supply."
